title: Knowledge Check 4: Lessons 16-20
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 16-20 of the ai-at-work series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Lesson 16 says the tool is not a decision-maker) what is it?
options: A generator of options, genuinely bad at telling you which option is good
A reliable chooser between well-formed options
A database of correct answers
An oracle that picks the best plan
questions.explanation: Lesson 16: the tool is a generator, not a chooser. It is very good at producing options and genuinely bad at telling you which option is good (the choosing stays with you.

questions.question: What is a 'premortem,' as Lesson 16 describes it?
options: A checklist of required tasks before a project starts
A stress-testing technique where you imagine the project has already failed and work backwards to explain why
A review of the project after it finishes
A financial forecast of project costs
questions.explanation: Lesson 16 cites Gary Klein's premortem: instead of asking 'what could go wrong,' you imagine the project has already failed and work backwards) prospective hindsight that makes it safe to name problems early.

questions.question: What did the Harvard Business School entrepreneur study cited in Lesson 16 conclude?
options: AI advice improved performance for everyone equally
The tool did not improve performance on its own; high performers picked specific suggestions while low performers took generic ones
Low performers improved more than high performers
The tool's advice was identical to a human consultant's
questions.explanation: Lesson 16: the AI business advisor boosted high performers by 10-15 percent and lowered low performers by ~8 percent. The difference was which advice users chose to follow: the judgment was what separated them.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Knowing When NOT to Use AI", which question should you start from?
options: Not "can I use AI for this," but "should I," because the answer to "can I" is almost always yes
"Can I use AI for this," because capability is the deciding factor
"Will the tool save money," regardless of the risk
"Has a competitor already automated this"
questions.explanation: The lesson says starting from can-I misleads you, because the tool can produce a draft for nearly anything you describe, which tells you nothing about whether you should use it.

questions.question: The lesson defines accountability. Which statement matches it?
options: Accountability transfers to the tool when the tool does the work
Accountability is yours even when a tool did the work, because the tool has no reputation, no job, no license, and no relationship to protect
Accountability only matters for legal or financial decisions
Accountability can be delegated along with the task itself
questions.explanation: The lesson says the tool cannot be accountable for anything, so whenever a task ends in something you own, the accountability stays with you, and that fact drives most of the lesson.

questions.question: How does the lesson define cost?
options: Only the price of the AI subscription
Only the time you spend typing the prompt
Your time, the risk of a wrong answer, the effort of checking, and the downside if the tool is confidently wrong
The number of tokens the model consumes
questions.explanation: The lesson widens cost past money and says the real question is whether the tool does the task better and more cheaply than the alternative once you count the checking.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Spotting the Automatable Tasks in Your Own Job", which question actually pays off?
options: Not whether your job is automatable, but which of the tasks in your job are automatable
Whether your whole occupation can be fully automated
Which of your colleagues' jobs are automatable
Whether the tool is cheaper than hiring someone
questions.explanation: The lesson says asking whether your job is automatable is too big to be useful, because a job is a bundle of dozens of small recurring tasks and only some of them are automatable.

questions.question: What research finding does the lesson cite about automation potential?
options: Most occupations can already be fully automated
Fewer than 5 percent of occupations could be fully automated with then-current technology, while about half of the activities people are paid to do had the technical potential to be automated
Automation potential is highest in the tasks that need the most judgment
Roughly 80 percent of occupations are fully automatable
questions.explanation: The lesson cites the McKinsey Global Institute work on activities rather than occupations, and uses it to argue that almost every job is a mix, so the real question is which slices are automatable.

questions.question: The lesson gives four signals of an automatable task. Which one belongs on that list?
options: The task is performed by more than one person
The task is highly visible to leadership
You can write the steps down and someone else, or a tool, could follow them without asking you a single question
The task takes at least a full working day
questions.explanation: That is the signal about writing the steps down, which the lesson pairs with frequency, and with the judgment call as its opposite: a decision that depends on context, values, or relationships you own is not a rule.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Building a Personal Prompt Library", what separates a pile of saved prompts from an actual library?
options: The metadata: a name, a phrase that says when to use it, and a note about what to check in the output
The software or app you store the prompts in
The total number of prompts in the collection
How long each prompt is
questions.explanation: The lesson says without the metadata you have a pile of prompts, and with it you have a library, because the metadata is what lets you find and use the right prompt.

questions.question: The lesson defines a "working prompt." What makes a prompt a working prompt?
options: It is long and highly detailed
It already produced an output you used and were happy with, so it has been tested in your actual job
It follows a formal template with placeholders
It was written by a colleague rather than by you
questions.explanation: The lesson says the word worked is doing the real work in that phrase: a working prompt has been tested in your job, not just imagined, which is what makes the library trustworthy.

questions.question: How does the lesson frame the payoff of building the library?
options: It removes the need to check outputs before you use them
It replaces your judgment with a saved template
Writing a good prompt from scratch costs thirty to sixty seconds every time plus the risk of forgetting a hard-won detail, and the library changes that math through compounding
It only pays off for tasks you perform twice a year
questions.explanation: The lesson works through the cost of rewriting a good prompt from memory for every recurring task and concludes the payoff shows up later, in the compounding.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Simple Repeatable Workflows You Can Run Weekly", what distinguishes a workflow from a prompt?
options: A prompt is one request, while a workflow is a fixed sequence of steps run in order toward a recurring result
A workflow requires software, while a prompt does not
A prompt produces better output than a workflow
A workflow has no output that needs checking
questions.explanation: The lesson draws the line plainly: a prompt is a single request, while a workflow is several requests arranged so each step hands its output to the next.

questions.question: What does the lesson say about the check step in a workflow?
options: It can be skipped once the workflow has proven stable
It is the step you never skip, because it is what keeps a fast routine safe, and it is where you decide
It is only needed for financial or legal workflows
It replaces the handoff between steps
questions.explanation: The lesson ties the check to the series-wide split that the tool drafts and you decide, and calls the check the place where that decision happens for a workflow.

questions.question: Why does the lesson insist on a timebox for a weekly workflow?
options: It makes the tool's output more accurate
It stops the tool from running for too long
Because a workflow you can finish in a set window actually runs every week, while one that balloons into an afternoon gets skipped
Because subscriptions are billed in time blocks
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the timebox as a fixed amount of time given to the workflow, like forty-five minutes on a Friday, and says the set window is what keeps it running.
